analysis.one_liner: Bars a single federal judge from issuing nationwide rulings; requires three-judge panels and random case assignment.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2023 with one sponsor and no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill responds to 'venue shopping' — the practice of filing a lawsuit in a district with a single judge who is likely to rule one way, then asking that one judge to block or erase a federal policy for the entire country. It would say no single district judge may grant nationwide relief, such as an injunction against the federal government or an order wiping out a federal regulation; a three-judge panel would have to hear the case instead. It would also require district courts to randomly assign cases so no single judge gets more than a 25 percent chance of any new case, and to publish how they divide cases among judges.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who relies on federal rules and protections — from drug approvals to worker and consumer regulations — gains stability, because one hand-picked judge could no longer freeze a national policy after a lawsuit filed in a chosen courtroom. Federal agencies also gain, since they could not see their work undone nationwide by a single district judge. Judge-shopping itself becomes far harder for every litigant, whatever their politics.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People relying on federal rules and protections

how_it_helps.text: A single district judge could no longer grant nationwide relief — an injunction against the federal government, an order vacating a federal regulation, or a stay of such relief — unless the case is heard by a three-judge district court panel [S3][S2].

District courts would have to ensure the chance a case lands on any particular judge does not exceed 25 percent, with a system of borrowing judges from adjacent districts in the same state where a district has too few judges [S3][S2].
District courts would have to publish, on their websites, the orders that spell out how cases are divided among judges, making the assignment rules visible to the public [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Any litigant — including advocacy groups and states on any side of an issue — who benefits from picking a favorable single judge to obtain a nationwide ruling loses that tool. Cases seeking nationwide relief also take longer, since three judges must hear them instead of one.
analysis.who_pays_short: Litigants who shop for favorable judges

drawbacks.text: Requiring three-judge panels and random assignment adds time and cost to lawsuits against the federal government, which can leave a contested policy in effect for months or years while the panel works [S3].

The restriction cuts both ways: a single judge's nationwide order has sometimes been the fastest way to stop a federal action that plaintiffs believed was unlawful, and this bill would slow that remedy down too [S3].

The bill leaves some loopholes by design: related cases, habeas petitions, and criminal proceedings are exempt from the random-assignment rule, so judge-picking remains possible in those categories [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but procedural: it removes a shortcut by which any group can pick one sympathetic judge and rewrite national policy from a single courtroom. The costs are slower justice and a somewhat weaker tool for anyone challenging the federal government, and the bill does not touch the Supreme Court or appeals courts, which can still issue nationwide relief. On balance it is a modest, good-government fix, though it addresses the symptom of forum shopping without solving the deeper question of when nationwide relief is proper at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and it stayed there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the bill on May 30, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5][S1].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor; the bill ended with zero cosponsors [S4].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Anyone who benefits from the status quo is better off: litigants of any political stripe can still file in a chosen district before a single judge likely to rule their way and ask for nationwide relief. The 25-percent random assignment rule and the three-judge requirement never took effect. Judicial administrators and district courts are also spared the workload of running three-judge panels and new assignment systems.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Litigants who can still shop for judges

against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the Congress, letting it die at the referral stage.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for anyone to vote on it: it had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no roll call, so no partisan lineup is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Litigants and advocacy groups that use forum shopping
industries.note: The bill's core target: parties who file suit in a single-judge district they expect to be friendly, then ask that judge to block or erase a federal policy nationwide, would lose that shortcut. Notable recent examples involved challenges to FDA approval of the abortion pill mifepristone, where a single district judge's order threatened nationwide access to a drug used by millions of patients.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and the federal government as defendant
industries.note: Agencies could no longer see their regulations vacated nationwide by one district judge, giving federal rules more stability. That stability reaches ordinary people who depend on those rules.

Courts would gain clearer rules against judge-picking but take on new work: convening three-judge panels, redesigning case assignment to meet the 25 percent cap, borrowing judges across districts, and publishing division orders.
